paragraphs: Canada's defence minister, David McGuinty, said on Saturday that people have been killed and injured in a large fire linked to an incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta. Speaking at a press conference that night, he said he was saddened to report both fatalities and injuries. He gave no casualty figures and no cause.

McGuinty described the situation as active and delicate and said he could not recall an incident like it in recent memory. According to The Guardian, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are involved in the investigation, and the armed forces and federal, provincial and local authorities are coordinating the response. The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire spread rapidly in high winds and crossed the base's fence. It said firefighters from multiple jurisdictions were responding, and the Guardian reported that no evacuation order was in effect.

Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency physician at Edmonton's Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city because Wainwright's health facilities were completely overwhelmed. He called the situation a disaster.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said a serious incident creating a major fire had occurred and that his thoughts were with those affected. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire significant and tragic. Saskatchewan and British Columbia offered help, and opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and McGuinty.

The base is one of Canada's busiest military training sites. The CBC said about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are there on a regular day. Large parts of Alberta were hit by a windstorm on Saturday, with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour. Officials have not yet said how many people were killed or hurt, or what started the fire.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Saturday that two oil tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's official IRNA news agency reported that the first ship's mine strike caused an explosion and a fierce fire, while the second ship was engulfed in a massive blaze. Al Jazeera said the ships' names and the origin of their cargo were not immediately available.

IRNA said the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route Iran had not authorised. The Guard also claimed that one tanker tried to cross with US support while the other was left immobilised. These claims come from Iranian sources and were not independently confirmed in the report.

Iran took control of the strait after the US-Israeli war on the country began in late February, and it has demanded that ships seek its approval before passing. About one-fifth of global oil consumption moved through the waterway before the war. This week an IRGC naval commander warned that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered hostile. The United States has imposed its own naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Attacks near the strait have surged over the past two weeks. Six vessels were attacked on Sunday, the most in a single day since the war began, according to Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the UK maritime agency UKMTO. Kpler data showed nearly 20.8 million barrels passing on October 8 but only 2.9 million on October 11. The disruption has pushed up global energy prices and inflation. President Donald Trump has said he believes a deal to end the war will come after the November 3 midterm elections.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Riyadh, the Eastern Province and the south of Saudi Arabia. Coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki made the announcement on Saturday. He also posted footage of what he described as the air force intercepting cruise missiles and drones and striking Houthi ballistic missile launchers.

Al Jazeera described the latest interceptions as part of a wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities. It reported that Riyadh's King Khalid airport has come under at least 20 attacks since fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government flared in July, including one last week that killed 13 people. On Thursday, at least five people died in missile strikes near the presidential palace in Aden, and the Yemeni government blamed the Houthis. The government said the Houthis fired two missiles at Aden's airport on Friday, while its forces said they advanced in Marib province.

Saudi Arabia is backing a government counteroffensive known as Dawn of Yemen and has carried out air strikes on the Houthis, including on an oil facility in Sanaa. Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthi escalation. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran supports a comprehensive political process as the only sustainable way to resolve the conflict.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said he was willing to carry out any measure to protect Saudi Arabia if the kingdom asked. He said Egypt was not seeking to intervene in regional wars and was speaking only about defence. Egypt's parliament holds an emergency session on Sunday at his request. Several embassies in Saudi Arabia have restricted travel and warned citizens not to use airports.

More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protests supporting high school students turned violent in several cities, according to Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. He said 150 police officers were hurt. The Guardian reported that hundreds of thousands marched peacefully, while violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.

The interior ministry said 550,000 people took part in marches, while the CGT union put the figure at 800,000. In Limoges, a fire set by masked protesters left the 143-year-old town hall largely lost, regional prefect Maurice Barate told AFP. Protesters entered the town hall in Marseille and broke into the one in Lille, and in Lyon the tourist office was set on fire. Police fired tear gas in Paris, where shops were looted. Paris mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said whole streets had been devastated.

President Emmanuel Macron said those responsible would be prosecuted and punished. Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said the state was not planning to declare a state of emergency. The protests began last month at schools in poor northern Paris suburbs over teacher absences and poor facilities, and widened into a movement over inequality, prices and public spending.

Political figures differed on blame. Marine Le Pen said Jean-Luc Mélenchon's party had legitimised the violence. Mélenchon had urged demonstrators to stay away from looting, calling it contrary to their methods. Al Jazeera reported cost-of-living protests the same day in Belgium, Italy and Portugal, with clashes in Brussels and Milan. An analyst told it more demonstrations could follow in other countries.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee demanded that Israel prosecute and jail those who attacked American photojournalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington wants Israel to do more to deter settler attacks. Al Jazeera reported both statements, made on Saturday.

Levine, 64, a photographer for The Washington Post, was covering the Palestinian olive harvest near Abu Falah on Friday. According to witnesses, Israeli settlers beat her and took her passport, phone, wallet and equipment. Levine said the attackers kicked her for about 10 minutes. Her daughter told The Associated Press that Levine had surgery on a nearly detached finger and suffered a broken rib, multiple broken vertebrae and lacerations.

Huckabee called the attack a despicable act of terror by masked cowards and said the US had called for a full investigation, arrest and prosecution. Rubio said he was very disturbed by images of the attack and that the State Department expected to hear back from the US embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. He said the Trump administration would tell Israel what it expects to prevent a repeat. The State Department's Friday statement condemned criminal violence by any party.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Palestinians or far-left activists may have been responsible, according to Al Jazeera. Al Jazeera said Huckabee did not name the culprits as settlers. Israel holds elections on October 27. Yesh Din, an Israeli monitoring group, counts at least 170 settler attacks on Palestinians since September 27. A fuller Israeli government response to the US demands was not included in the report.

Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has joined a new political-military coalition challenging President Felix Tshisekedi, Al Jazeera reported from Goma. The Front pour la Refondation de la Nation, known as the FRN, was announced in Goma on Monday evening. It is led by Kabila and replaces the existing alliance between the Alliance Fleuve Congo and the M23 movement.

According to the report, the coalition accuses Tshisekedi of tyranny and calls for resistance by all means, including force. M23 and the Alliance Fleuve Congo have controlled Goma, the main city in North Kivu province, since January last year. The conflict has displaced millions and drawn in neighbouring countries. The Congolese government and international actors accuse Rwanda of backing M23, which Kigali denies, citing security threats from armed groups in eastern Congo.

Goma resident Basa Juhudi told Al Jazeera that Kabila's move means the war is far from over. Vital Kamerhe, a former speaker of the National Assembly, said nothing can justify taking up weapons against the country and urged the movement's leaders to choose dialogue. Kabila took power in 2001, was elected in 2006 and 2011, and his second term was due to end in 2016. Elections were delayed until December 2018, and critics accused him of trying to stay in power. Tshisekedi took office in 2019.

The United States has pursued a DRC-Rwanda agreement, and Qatar has hosted talks between the Congolese government and AFC-M23 on a ceasefire and other measures. Al Jazeera said Kabila's role raises questions about who will represent the armed opposition and whether existing commitments will hold. The FRN has said it intends to honour commitments made in the Doha talks. Whether Kabila can build wider support remains uncertain.

Vice President JD Vance said he will have to decide on a 2028 presidential run after the midterm elections. He spoke at a CBS News town hall in Michigan, hosted by Tony Dokoupil, which aired Saturday night. Asked whether there is a chance he will not run, he said of course there is, noting that he has four young children and calling himself a procrastinator. He said that after Republican Mike Rogers is elected to the Senate in Michigan, he will have to think about it, but added that anything can happen.

Gas prices were the first topic. Vance said Iran's attacks on commercial shipping had disrupted energy markets, and he also said about 20 percent of US refining capacity went offline under President Biden. He said the administration is using the Defense Production Act to help restore it but that this will take time. Dokoupil noted that Vance and President Trump have been in office for nearly two years. Vance also acknowledged that gas prices are too high.

On corruption, Dokoupil cited a Fox News poll showing 60 percent of voters extremely concerned. Vance said he sees evidence of corruption in Washington but not from the president or the administration. He said selling access would be disgusting and despicable and that he would comply with subpoenas if Democrats take Congress. On immigration, he said that to the extent his rhetoric was imperfect, that was on him, while defending his criticism of companies that use the H-1B visa system.

On Iran, Vance said the US has destroyed Iran's nuclear program and in some ways has won decisively. The White House, he said, is now seeking a deal to keep Iran from rebuilding and a long-term fix for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said US military aid to Israel should come with conditions, and he called that quickly becoming the consensus position of the Democratic Party. He made the comments to the Washington Examiner on Saturday in Manchester, New Hampshire, where he campaigned for state and congressional candidates and is weighing a 2028 presidential run.

Newsom pointed to settler violence and conditions in the West Bank. He said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies preclude any chance of a two-state solution, which he said is against the interests of the American people. He called the war in Gaza a moral catastrophe and said Netanyahu had isolated himself from the world and increasingly from Americans. He said the outcome of Israel's October 27 election would play a big role.

Newsom declined to detail which aid should be conditioned, though he distinguished between defensive systems such as the Iron Dome and the bombs and munitions Israel receives. He cited the Leahy framework and human rights principles as the foundation for conditions.

The Examiner described his remarks as among his most pointed yet. It noted that in the spring most of the Senate's 47 Democrats voted to block a weapons sale to Israel, and more than 100 House Democrats voted against a separate measure in July. In March, Newsom said he regretted endorsing the view that Israel had become an apartheid state. The article said other expected 2028 hopefuls have gone further, with some saying the US should stop the $3.8 billion in annual aid. It added that Netanyahu has proposed weaning Israel off the aid over a decade and that some Republicans agree. No Israeli government or Republican response to Newsom's comments was reported.

Arizona has joined Nevada in a legal fight against the Trump administration's proposed cuts to their shares of the Colorado River, according to The Guardian. Governor Katie Hobbs announced the move in a Friday statement.

The step follows restrictions announced by the Interior Department this summer. They could reduce water supplied to the lower basin states of Arizona, California and Nevada over the next two years, depending on the river's condition. The reservoirs Lake Mead and Lake Powell have fallen to historically low levels, which the Guardian attributes to overuse and a changing climate.

The states that share the river had been at an impasse. Upper basin states argued that downstream states were responsible for the shortages and should face the largest cuts. The federal government stepped in after the states missed several deadlines for a consensus. The upper basin states of Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico were spared from the cuts, an exemption that has drawn sharp criticism from lower basin leaders.

Hobbs said: "We are drawing a line in the sand." She said she was acting with Nevada because the federal government "refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they owe Arizona." She said it is threatening cuts that go beyond the Lower Basin Agreement, a two-year voluntary conservation pact among Arizona, California and Nevada.

Tom Buschatzke, director of Arizona's water department, said joining the Nevada lawsuit was necessary to protect the state's legal rights while keeping open a path to a collaborative outcome with California and Nevada. An Interior Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, so the department's response to the litigation was not reported.

Trudy strengthened to a Category 2 hurricane on Saturday as it moved toward Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, the US National Hurricane Center said. A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco.

The latest data showed maximum sustained winds of 100mph. The storm was about 205 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes and 115 miles south-southwest of Manzanillo, moving northwest at 10mph. Its center was expected to approach the coast on Saturday and pass near it into Sunday. Mexico's government issued a tropical storm warning for Las Islas Marias and discontinued a similar warning for its coast south of Lazaro Cardenas.

The Mexican navy urged mariners and coastal residents to use extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides. Colima authorities said the risks remained low but warned that heavy rain could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms. Trudy was expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of about 15 inches.

Elsewhere in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi strengthened into a Category 4 storm moving west toward Guam. By Saturday night local time it was about 25 miles southeast of Guam with winds of 140mph, according to the US National Weather Service. It was forecast to pass south of Guam early Sunday and keep intensifying. Guam and Rota were under a typhoon warning, while Tinian and Saipan were under a tropical storm warning and typhoon watch.

The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday. Approval by Donald Trump would authorize federal support and funding. FEMA said resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days. The territories are still recovering from Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July.

Two people, including a child, were killed during a soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, when a person drove a vehicle through the field at the Stryker soccer complex, police confirmed. Multiple other people were injured, according to The Guardian.

Aaron Moses of the Wichita police department said at a Saturday news conference that the driver is in custody and that two juveniles were in the vehicle. Police said one child was killed at the scene and one adult also died. They did not release names or ages until family could be notified. Those hurt were taken to hospitals, but the extent of their injuries is unknown. "This is a tragedy," Moses said.

Moses said he did not know how fast the vehicle was traveling or how it got onto the field. Officials are still investigating. The city said all events at the soccer complex are canceled until further notice, and police have set up a portal for anyone to submit video of the incident.

A witness told local station KWCH that a black pickup truck was seen "plowing through the youth soccer fields." The witness said the truck hit multiple people before stopping 100 to 200 yards down the fields. They reported seeing dozens of emergency responders giving aid and CPR to victims. That account came from a witness, and police have not confirmed those details.

Wichita Mayor Lily Wu posted on social media that she was "heartbroken by reports of a tragic incident at Stryker Sports Complex," adding that her thoughts and prayers were with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved. Further details are expected as the investigation continues, including the identities of the victims and the condition of the injured.

The Falkland Islands are facing what a local lawmaker describes as an unprecedented economic campaign from Argentina, according to The Guardian. Assembly member Lewis Clifton told islanders at a Monday evening question session that the level of Argentine pressure was "at a different level," perhaps with "a more vehement and belligerent tone" than since 1982, because it could threaten the islands' economic development.

The Guardian reports that Argentine President Javier Milei, who faces a downturn in domestic polling and an upcoming election, has legislated to criminalize companies and individuals involved in the Falklands' nascent oil industry. He has also suggested the fisheries industry, on which the islands' current prosperity rests, could be next. The Guardian says British forces at Mount Pleasant make a military threat largely hypothetical. Argentina's response to this account was not included in the article.

In response this week, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband restated solidarity with the islanders' wish to remain British and promised legislation that might offer some protection against financial damage from Argentina's sanctions. The Foreign Office also made representations asking Interpol to reject an Argentine request for arrests relating to the dispute. Clifton called the stance "catching up time." Resident Norma Edwards, 84, said she had never trusted the Foreign Office.

The islands' economy has changed since the 1982 war. The Guardian says the population was 1,800 four decades ago and now includes about 70 nationalities, with a 26% top tax rate and a self-reliant economy. John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association, said squid had been "transformational." A residency scheme capped at 90 people a year has been frozen for 12 months. The Guardian says the situation remains precarious.

Lena Schilling, an Austrian Green member of the European Parliament, has spoken publicly about discovering nude deepfakes of herself online and has urged the EU to act, The Guardian reports. A new report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content.

Schilling said she learned last month that the images were circulating. They were altered versions of photos from one of her first press conferences, with her clothing digitally removed. "I felt disgusted," she said. She called the images "digital violence against women" and a threat to democracy, saying such abuse makes politics harder and could push more women out of public life.

According to a report by the Berlin-based thinktank Agora Digitale Transformation, which alerted Schilling, 50 MEPs, 46 of them women, have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes. The group called this a "systemic threat to women in European politics." An earlier report by the group found that 138 female parliamentarians from 22 EU countries had been affected, and that women were 33 times more likely than male colleagues to be depicted in or linked to deepfake pornography.

Schilling and German Green MEP Terry Reintke initiated a letter signed by 119 MEPs. It asks that a forthcoming EU ban on apps and websites that use AI to undress women, scheduled to take effect on 2 December, be paired with ways to enforce it. "A ban on paper protects no one until it is enforced," the letter said.

Schilling said she wants national authorities to close loopholes that would let such apps keep working in the EU. She said she spoke out hoping member states would crack down on tech companies for which this kind of abuse could be a viable business model. She said other targeted MEPs had feared coming forward, and added: "There's nothing to be ashamed of."

A BBC report from Columbus, Ohio, and Chicago describes how homemade synthetic drugs are changing the US drug crisis. Overdose deaths peaked at 110,000 in 2022, mostly from opioids, and have since fallen to around 70,000 last year, the BBC says. It adds that this does not mean the opioid crisis is over.

The BBC says fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin and is now often cut with synthetic tranquilizers such as xylazine and medetomidine. These animal sedatives slow breathing and are not reversed by naloxone, the nasal spray whose wide adoption the BBC credits with sharply reducing fatal overdoses. Xylazine also causes deep necrotic skin ulcers that are hard to treat. The report says cocktails can be made in American basements and bathtubs.

The reporters spent days with Mike, a 48-year-old army veteran who smokes fentanyl in Columbus. A drug kit he brought to a sampling program tested positive for medetomidine. The program, run with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention by the recovery group Hope Dealer Community, sends samples to a CDC laboratory in North Carolina.

Scott Sanders, who runs the group, said 78% of fatal overdoses in Franklin County over the past 12 months involved stimulants. He said crack users often believe they are buying only crack but are getting it mixed with fentanyl or other drugs, which he said is called a "hot dose" on the street. He said overdose deaths among Black men in Ohio are increasing.

In Chicago, the BBC spoke to a dealer who works for Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He said he knows his work is wrong, but argued that the end justifies the means. The BBC links basement-made synthetics to a dramatic rise in overdose deaths in Illinois.

London's Metropolitan Police said on Saturday that no further action will be taken over a social media post by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, that appeared to endorse Palestine Action. A spokesperson said specialist officers assessed the post and determined it "did not meet the criminal threshold."

Helm, a journalist and author, wrote on X on Thursday: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action." The Guardian reports it is understood there was insufficient evidence that the post was capable of encouraging support for a proscribed organization. The police had said on Friday that the post was being assessed.

Helm was responding to a discussion about Irish author Sally Rooney. Publisher Faber said this week that, because of current UK legislation, it cannot pass on UK earnings to Rooney, who announced plans to use royalties to support Palestine Action. Faber said it had agreed with her to stop supplying her works in the UK, while continuing sales elsewhere.

Palestine Action has been proscribed as a terrorist organization since a July 2025 vote by UK lawmakers. Membership or support is an offense punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested for allegedly supporting the group, many for holding placards. The group challenged the ban, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that it was lawful.

The Campaign Against Antisemitism had urged police to investigate, saying that while spouses are entitled to independent views, the post raised "extremely serious questions" for Powell and the government. A government spokesperson said Helm holds her views as an individual who "does not represent the government in any capacity." Helm's own response was not included in the reports.

An incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while in labor last weekend, according to the advocacy group Sisters Inside, as reported by The Guardian. The group's chief executive, Debbie Kilroy, said the woman gave birth by caesarean section to a premature baby and had been "shackled on and off since she came into the hospital."

Kilroy said hospital staff called Sisters Inside after trying to get the shackles removed, and that some were crying because prison staff would not remove them. She said the woman's health was deteriorating and that the shackles came off on Friday. A Queensland corrective services spokesperson confirmed a woman had been shackled in labor and said the incident would face an internal review, because restraints are only meant to be used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners where necessary to maintain public safety.

The birth came days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a bill from independent senator Lidia Thorpe to ban shackling of incarcerated women during childbirth. Thorpe also introduced a bill to stop children being strip-searched. The government said this week that criminal justice is a matter for states and territories. The Coalition said it understood the intent but would not support the bill. Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr said he was "deeply concerned" and would raise the issue with the Queensland attorney general.

Thorpe said the commonwealth has the constitutional power to set a national standard and is choosing not to. She asked how many more women "have to go through this horrific experience before the Albanese government acts." The Guardian notes that Australia has signed the UN Bangkok rules, which say restraints "shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth."

Satellite images analyzed by the BBC show an 80-meter luxury vessel repeatedly seen off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October. Its most distinctive feature is a 50-meter swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, the vessel moved in early July to waters off the Kalma Peninsula, close to Wonsan, where leader Kim Jong Un and his family have a sprawling villa. The BBC tracked three other large vessels of about 50, 55 and 60 meters, all repeatedly seen near the villa this year. The BBC says they are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family, and former officials, defectors and experts say it would be hard for anyone outside the leadership to own or freely use such ships. North Korea has never publicly disclosed their ownership.

Ri Jong Ho, a former official of the Workers' Party's Office 39, said the vessels are kept at the shipyard in winter and moved to Kim's villa or Kalma in summer for recreation. The BBC says vessel locations cannot prove where the family is, but their movements overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances. A BBC analysis found a vessel with the same characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled.

The BBC contrasts this with conditions for ordinary North Koreans. A 2025 UN report says an estimated 40% of the population is undernourished, and per capita GDP was around $667 in 2024. Workers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, defectors said, but this is rarely followed, and travel outside a city or county requires official permission.
State media rarely reports on Kim being on holiday, presenting such visits as official inspections. The Wonsan Kalma resort opened in July 2025 and has hosted small groups of Russian tourists.

Bolotana, a mountain village of 2,266 people in central Sardinia, could become the world's sixth "blue zone," an area with an unusually high concentration of centenarians, The Guardian reports. Unlike the first such zone, also in Sardinia, the pattern here is driven by women.

A study by researchers at the University of Sassari and the University of Alabama at Birmingham, published in Frontiers in Aging last week, found that 13.8% of women in Bolotana who reach 70 will live to 100. That places the village second in the world for female longevity, after Hong Kong. Records of people born there between 1900 and 1925 showed 38 lived beyond 100, a rate 57% above the Italian average. The village now has six female centenarians, and the last male centenarian died in July.

Giovanni Mario Pes, who led the study and co-created the blue zone concept, said this is the first area identified where women live to a great age, whereas the original zone was predominantly male. Scientists are tracing family trees for genetic clues and exploring diet, physical activity and social connections. Bolotana's steep streets provide daily exercise, and many residents eat fruit and vegetables from their gardens.

Pes also noted a "strong sense of sisterhood" among the women and said he would like to explore it scientifically. Mayor Francesco Manconi said natural affection from family, neighbors and friends toward the elderly is key, and that the village prioritizes letting them stay in their own homes.

The women profiled are notably independent. Giovanna Marras, 101, and her sister Mariangela, 99, still cook for themselves and eat meat, cheese and wine. Filomena Scarpa, 100, began learning German in her 90s and sees a personal trainer twice a week.
